content.title: About
content.content: Shortbread is a traditional Scottish biscuit made from butter, sugar, flour and sometimes a pinch of salt. It has a dense, crumbly texture and a delicate buttery flavor with a hint of sweetness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shortbread originated in Scotland in the 18th century and was a favorite of the royal family.
It is traditionally cut into rectangular or round pieces, often dusted with powdered sugar.
The classic recipe uses only butter, with no leavening agents.
In the United States shortbread is often called “butter cookies” and used as a base for desserts such as cheesecakes.
Many variations exist, adding nuts, dried fruit, chocolate or spices.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates and fats provide a quick source of energy.

items.title: Contains vitamins A and D
items.content: Butter supplies vitamins A and D, important for vision and bone health.

items.title: Provides calcium
items.content: Calcium supports healthy bones and teeth.

items.title: Small amount of iron
items.content: Iron contributes to oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Flour adds a modest amount of fiber, beneficial for digestion.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Butter may trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Shortbread is rich in fats and sugars, so it should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: High sugar levels can contribute to tooth decay and raise blood glucose.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Flour contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Shortbread can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, served with tea or coffee, used as a base for desserts, crumbled over ice cream, or sprinkled on cupcakes. It can also be gently warmed to enhance the buttery aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store shortbread in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life keep it in the refrigerator to prevent the butter from turning rancid. Discard if it develops a stale smell or off‑texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Oyster crackers are light, crunchy snack crackers made from wheat flour, vegetable oil, and seasonings that mimic the taste of sea oysters. They have a mild salty note and a distinctive marine aroma, perfect for pairing with cheeses, dips, and soups.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first oyster‑flavored cracker recipe appeared in the United States in the early 20th century.
Oyster crackers are often used as a non‑alcoholic alternative to seafood appetizers.
Their sodium content is usually lower than that of traditional salty chips.
Natural seaweed extracts are used to achieve the characteristic flavor.
Oyster crackers are commonly served in bars and restaurants as a beer accompaniment.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many snack foods, these crackers contain a modest amount of fat, making them a lighter choice.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Wheat flour provides slow‑releasing energy, helping to maintain satiety.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 supports protein metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Crackers contain small amounts of iron, magnesium, and zinc, essential for metabolic processes.

items.title: Suitable for diet plans
items.content: Their low calorie density allows inclusion in weight‑control diets.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Made from wheat flour, these crackers can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Although moderate, individuals on low‑salt diets should monitor portion size.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some versions may contain food preservatives that are not suitable for all consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Oyster crackers can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, served with cheese, pâté, creamy dips, or used as a base for canapés. They also add a pleasant crunch when sprinkled over salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep crackers in a sealed package in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. For extended storage, refrigerate to preserve crispness and flavor.

infant-formula-enfamil-prosobee-powder-m.title: Infant formula, Enfamil ProSobee, powder, prepared with tap water

content.title: About
content.content: Enfamil ProSobee is a hypoallergenic infant formula powder designed for babies at risk of developing allergies. It contains partially hydrolyzed soy protein, prebiotics, DHA, ARA, and essential vitamins and minerals. Preparation is done with clean tap water according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: ProSobee is one of the few formulas where the soy protein is partially hydrolyzed, reducing its allergenic potential.
The formula is enriched with prebiotics (FOS) that support the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.
It includes DHA and ARA – fatty acids important for brain and eye development.
The product has a neutral taste, making the transition from breast milk to formula easier.
Enfamil ProSobee has undergone clinical testing confirming its safety for infants with a family history of allergies.

items.title: Reduced allergy risk
items.content: Partially hydrolyzed soy protein is less likely to trigger allergic reactions, helping prevent food allergies in susceptible infants.

items.title: Brain development support
items.content: DHA and ARA contribute to neuronal connectivity and visual function during early growth.

items.title: Immune system support
items.content: Vitamins A, C, D and zinc help maintain a healthy immune response in babies.

items.title: Gut health
items.content: Prebiotics (FOS) stimulate beneficial bacteria, improving digestion and nutrient absorption.

items.title: Growth nourishment
items.content: A balanced blend of proteins, fats, and carbohydrates provides the energy and building blocks needed for healthy growth.

items.title: Soy protein allergy
items.content: Although hydrolyzed, some infants may still react to soy components.

items.title: Water quality
items.content: Using tap water requires that the water meets safety standards; otherwise there is a risk of microbial contamination.

items.title: Incorrect dilution
items.content: Over‑concentrated or overly diluted formula can lead to dehydration or over‑feeding, negatively affecting the infant’s health.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The formula contains a small amount of sugar for palatability; caregivers should monitor intake in children prone to dental caries.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Mix the specified amount of powder into clean boiled (or filtered) water that has been cooled to body temperature (≈37 °C). Stir thoroughly to eliminate lumps. The prepared feed should be used within 2 hours and should not be stored in the refrigerator for more than 24 hours.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry powder in its original airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, use within 3 months. Do not keep prepared formula for more than 24 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Kidney beans and rice is a popular fast‑food dish often served in Mexican and Latin‑American restaurants. The combination of cooked beans (red or brown) with fluffy rice provides a hearty, nutrient‑dense meal that can be easily customized with various toppings and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish emerged in the United States in the early 20th century as an inexpensive lunch option for factory workers.
Traditionally the beans are simmered with tomato sauce, spices, and sometimes topped with cheese or guacamole.
Beans and rice together form a complete protein, compensating for each other's limiting amino acids.
In some regions the meal is served with corn chips or fresh salsa on the side.
Kidney beans and rice are a staple in school cafeterias because of their affordability and nutritional profile.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: The bean‑rice combo provides all essential amino acids, making it a solid meat alternative.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Beans supply soluble and insoluble fiber that supports digestion and blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are important for oxygen transport, energy production, and muscle function.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When prepared with minimal oil, the dish fits well into heart‑healthy eating patterns.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beans and rice are good sources of thiamine, niacin, and folate, which aid metabolism and nervous‑system health.

items.title: Gas‑producing beans
items.content: Some people experience digestive discomfort from beans; soaking and thorough cooking can reduce this effect.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Restaurant versions often contain added salt and sauces, raising the sodium level.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small percentage of individuals may be allergic to beans.

items.title: High glycemic index of white rice
items.content: White rice can cause a rapid blood‑sugar spike; using brown rice offers a steadier response.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, typically in a portioned bowl. It can be topped with salsa, guacamole, shredded cheese, fresh cilantro, or a squeeze of lime. For a lighter version, choose brown rice and limit added salt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked beans and rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat to at least 75 °C before eating. Frozen portions retain quality for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato hash brown with cheese is a crispy patty made from grated potatoes, fried to a golden crust and topped with melted cheese. The dish is popular in restaurants as a quick, satisfying snack, combining the mild flavor of potato with the richness of cheese.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hash browns originated in Eastern European cuisine, where they were traditionally made from potatoes and onions.
Adding cheese makes the dish more nutritious and gives it a creamy taste.
Many restaurants serve hash browns with a variety of sauces: sour cream, tartar sauce, or tomato salsa.
Potato hash browns are often used as a base for breakfast, lunch, or dinner plates.
There are many variations: with bacon, herbs, mushrooms, or even seafood.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Potatoes provide slowly digestible carbs that supply steady energy and help maintain blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Potatoes contain vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus from cheese
items.content: Cheese adds calcium and phosphorus, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Protein
items.content: The combination of potato and cheese increases the protein content, aiding tissue repair.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: If whole‑grain flour or bran is added to the batter, the fiber content rises, benefiting digestion.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Frying and cheese make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese contains saturated fats, which can affect cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Lactose
items.content: People with lactose intolerance should choose lactose‑free cheese or limit the amount.

items.title: Salt
items.content: Cheese is often salty; those with high blood pressure should reduce added salt.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hash browns hot, straight from the pan, to keep the crust crunchy. They can be enjoyed on their own or with sour cream, yogurt dip, or fresh herbs. For a lighter option, bake the hash browns in the oven.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked hash browns in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Frozen hash browns keep well for up to 3 months; reheat in the oven or skillet before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Tomato cream soup is a ready‑to‑eat puree soup made from ripe tomatoes, cream, and aromatic spices. It has a smooth, velvety texture with a gentle sweet‑tart tomato flavor balanced by a subtle creamy note.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tomatoes used are often greenhouse‑grown, allowing a consistent flavor year‑round.
Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that gives them their bright red color.
Creamy tomato soups originated in France in the early 20th century.
The soup is commonly garnished with croutons, fresh herbs, or a drizzle of olive oil.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Lycopene helps protect cells from oxidative stress and supports heart health.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Tomatoes provide vitamin C, which contributes to immune system function.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: The creamy texture and modest fiber content make it easy to digest.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A 250 ml serving contains about 80 kcal, making it suitable for weight‑conscious diets.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Tomatoes supply vitamin B6 and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes or added spices.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared soup can contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Tomatoes are naturally acidic, which may cause discomfort for those with gastritis or reflux.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot; you can add a swirl of cream, croutons, fresh basil, or grated Parmesan. If desired, thin with water or broth to reach your preferred consistency.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened package refrigerated at +2…+4 °C for up to 5 days. Once opened, consume within 2‑3 days. The soup can be frozen in an airtight container for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Vodka is a distilled spirit made from fermented grains (wheat, rye, barley) or potatoes. Its clean taste, neutral aroma, and typical 40 % ABV make it a base for countless cocktails and a traditional drink in Russia and Eastern Europe.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “vodka” derives from the Russian “voda” meaning water, emphasizing its purity.
Industrial vodka production began in Russia in the mid‑19th century.
Traditional vodka is filtered through charcoal, which smooths the spirit.
Popular serving methods include neat shots over ice or in cocktails such as the Martini and Cosmopolitan.
Some countries require vodka to be unflavored, while others allow flavored varieties.

items.title: Moderate consumption may promote relaxation
items.content: Small amounts of alcohol have a sedative effect, helping to reduce stress and anxiety.

items.title: Contains trace antioxidants in some grain‑based vodkas
items.content: Vodka made from whole grains can contain low levels of polyphenols, which have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Alcohol dependence
items.content: Regular consumption of vodka can lead to addiction and serious health problems.

items.title: Liver disease risk
items.content: Excessive intake damages the liver and may cause cirrhosis.

items.title: Cardiovascular effects
items.content: High doses raise blood pressure and increase the risk of stroke.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Alcohol can amplify the effects of sedatives and reduce the efficacy of certain drugs.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Vodka is usually served chilled, either as a shot or mixed into cocktails. It can also be used in marinades, sauces, or desserts, but its high alcohol content should be considered.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the bottle in a cool, dark place with the cap tightly sealed. Avoid direct sunlight during long storage to prevent flavor changes.
